• Scientific name: Pterobunocephalus depressus (Haseman, 1911)
  • Common name: Banjo Catfish
  • Type locality: Río Machupo near San Joaquín, Amazon system, Bolivia.
  • Synonyms: Buncephalus depressus, Bunocephalus albofasciatus
  • Size: 89 mm (3.5") SL.
  • Identification: Smaller than Bunocephalus species and can most readily be distinguished from that genus by the number of anal fin rays (11-20 in Pterobunocephalus vs. 5-10 in Bunocephalus).

Family: Aspredinidae. Size: 9.0 cm. Temperature: 25-28°C. pH: 6.0-8.0.

IUCN Red List: despite the limited information available on this species, it is assessed as Least Concern due to its wide range (IUCN 2021).
South America: Amazon, Orinoco and Paraguay River basins.
South America: Amazon, Orinoco and Paraguay River basins. Type locality: Todos Santos, Bolivia.
Small species that can probably be kept as per other members of this family with a quiet tank with sand and plants.
Breeding: unreported. There is no breeding report.
Females of this genus carry embryos directly attached to the ventral surface of their bodies, which also distinguishes them from all other aspredinids.

Pterobunocephalus is a genus of small to medium sized aspredinid species. Members of this genus are distinguished from all other aspredinids by the following characters: an extremely depressed (flattened) head and body, highly reduced or absent head ornamentation, often a distinct notch in the upper jaw, and 10–20 anal fin rays.

Etymology: the genus name Pterobunocephalus: pterus, referring to the large anal fin of Bunocephalus (subgenus Pterobunocephalus) albifasciatus (= P. depressus). The specific name depressus: referring to its “greatly depressed” body.
